$1,500 and 200 thousand apartments

before.feedback: A nonbinding ceiling leaves equilibrium unchanged.

questions.reason: Identify equilibrium, diagnose nonbinding ceiling and reversed shortage sign, then infer the corresponding binding floor.

before.q: A student uses the quantities shown at the $2,000 rent ceiling to conclude that the market has a surplus. What is the student’s error?
options: A ceiling is a minimum, so price must remain above 2,000 dollars
The displayed quantities must be added instead of subtracted
A ceiling is a maximum, so price can clear below 2,000 dollars
Any price above equilibrium necessarily creates a shortage
before.feedback: A ceiling is a maximum, not a mandated price.

after.q: Refer to the graph. A student says a $2,000 rent ceiling binds and creates a 200-thousand-apartment shortage. Which diagnosis corrects both errors and identifies the policy that could sustain the gap at $2,000?
options: Binding ceiling: $2,000 and 100 thousand; Qd > Qs by 200 thousand, consistent with a binding floor.
Nonbinding ceiling: $1,500 and 200 thousand; at $2,000, Qd > Qs by 200 thousand, consistent with a binding ceiling.
Nonbinding ceiling: $1,500 and 200 thousand; at $2,000, Qs > Qd by 200 thousand, consistent with a binding floor.
Binding ceiling: $2,000 and 300 thousand; Qs > Qd by 200 thousand, consistent with a binding ceiling.
after.feedback: Equilibrium is $1,500 and 200 thousand. A maximum of $2,000 permits that equilibrium and does not force price up. At $2,000, Qs=300 thousand and Qd=100 thousand: the hypothetical gap is a 200-thousand surplus. A floor at $2,000, not the stated ceiling, could hold price above equilibrium.

questions.reason: Diagnose the minimum-price, employment and gap-sign errors, then distinguish a floor from a ceiling.

before.q: Refer to the graph. A student treats the $6 minimum wage as the market wage and predicts a labor shortage. What is the student’s error?
options: A floor is a minimum, so wage can rise to equilibrium
A floor is a maximum, so wage cannot rise above 6 dollars
Labor supply must be subtracted from equilibrium quantity
Any wage below equilibrium creates a binding surplus
before.feedback: A floor is a minimum, not a mandated wage.

after.q: Refer to the graph. A student says a $6 minimum wage binds, fixes employment at 300 thousand and creates a 200-thousand-worker surplus. Which diagnosis corrects the claim and identifies the policy that could sustain the gap at $6?
options: Nonbinding floor: $12 and 200 thousand; at $6, Qd > Qs by 200 thousand, consistent with a binding wage ceiling.
Binding floor: $6 and 300 thousand; Qs > Qd by 200 thousand, consistent with a binding wage ceiling.
Nonbinding floor: $12 and 200 thousand; at $6, Qs > Qd by 200 thousand, consistent with a binding wage floor.
Binding floor: $6 and 100 thousand; Qd > Qs by 200 thousand, consistent with a binding wage floor.
after.feedback: The $6 minimum is below the $12 equilibrium, so wage and employment remain $12 and 200 thousand. At a hypothetical $6 wage, firms demand 300 thousand workers but only 100 thousand offer labor: a shortage, not surplus. A binding wage ceiling could prevent wage from rising; the floor does not.
